Culture of cell lines
HG3 cells (purchased from DSMZ #ACC 765) were cultured in RPMI 1640 (Gibco #11875-093) with 15% fetal bovine serum (FBS) (Sigma-Aldrich ), 1% GlutaMAX (Gibco, cat# 35050-061) and 1% penicillin-streptomycin (Life Technologies). Cells were incubated at 37 °C, 5% CO2 and passaged every 48 hours. All subsets of the HG3 cell line were also cultured under these conditions. Cells were routinely tested for mycoplasma per the manufacturer’s instructions (VenorGeM Mycoplasma Detection Kit; Sigma-Aldrich #MP0025).

Generation of mutant human CLL cell lines
Sleeping Beauty transposon plasmids carrying one of four RPS15 CLL mutations (G134R or c.400 G>C; H137Y or c.409C>T; S138F or c.413 C>T; and S139F or c.416 C>T) or the RPS15 WT gene were assembled by introducing gBlocks® (IDT) containing a Flag and HA tag upstream of the RPS15 WT or mutant coding sequence (codon optimized using the IDT Codon Optimization Tool), with SfiI overhangs on each end. Cloning was performed by digesting both the Sleeping Beauty inducible transposon plasmid pSBtet-GP (Addgene plasmid #60495; contains GFP and puromycin selection markers) (125) and each gBlock with SfiI (#R0123S, New England Biolabs). To generate RPS15 mutant HG3 cell lines, HG3 cells were electroporated with 15 µg of pCMV(CAT)T7-SB100 (transposase, Addgene #34879) and 15 µg of each of the mutant transposon vectors. Successfully transposed cells were purified twice by FACS post-nucleofection.

To generate cells compatible with the CRISPR-Cas9 system, lentivirus was generated by co-transfection of LentiCas9-Blast (Addgene #52962) (126) along with pMD2.G (Addgene #12259) and psPAX2 (Addgene #12260) into HEK 293T using Lipofectamine 2000 (Life Technologies). Supernatant containing lentiviral particles was collected at 48 and 72 hours and concentrated using Lenti-X (Clontech). HG3 cells were transduced with fresh lentivirus in the presence of 8 g/mL polybrene and selected by blasticidine (20 μg/ml) for two weeks and Cas9 activity was tested using a previously reported system (127). We generated TP53 knockout HG3 cell lines as previously described (128). sgRNAs were designed using the online CRISPR design tool (http://crispr.mit.edu/) to target TP53. The selection of the sgRNAs was based on choosing those of highest efficiency to target the gene of interest and with the lowest predicted off-targets effects. The sgRNA targeting TP53 (5’-CCATTGTTCAATATCGTCCG-3’) was cloned into pLKO5.sgRNA.EFS.tRFP (Addgene_#57823). Cloning was carried out as previously described (128) and lentivirus was generated as described above. Cas9-expressing HG3 cells were transduced with the above TP53-targeting construct and RFP+ cells were flow-sorted as single cells into 96-well plates. To confirm CRISPR editing of the TP53 loci, gDNA was extracted using the QIAampDNA Micro Kit (Qiagen) following the manufacturer’s instructions. PCR was performed using primers flanking the target sites for the sgRNAs (Forward: AGACCTGTGGGAAGCGAAAA; Reverse: GACAGGAAGCCAAAGGGTGA). For screening the loss-of-function mutations, PCR products were purified using High Pure PCR Product Purification Kit (Roche) and resulting indels at the expected locations were confirmed by Sanger sequencing. The efficiency of the sgRNAs was assessed by Tracking of Indels by Decomposition (TIDE) software (https://tide-calculator.nki.nl; Netherlands Cancer Institute). Western blots were performed to confirm loss of p53 expression as described above (Western Blot).

Quantitative PCR
Total gDNA or RNA was extracted from HG3 cells using the DNeasy Blood & Tissue Kit (QIAGEN) and the RNA purification kit (QIAGEN), respectively. To make cDNA, 2 µg of RNA was reverse-transcribed into cDNA using the SuperscriptII reverse transcription kit (Life Technologies). mRNA or gDNA templates were quantified using the TaqMan Gene Expression Assay probes (Thermo Fisher): RPS15 (Hs01358643_g1), GAPDH (4333764T), and a customized TaqMan probe specific to the codon-optimized RPS15 transgene (RPS15_PCW, Assay ID #APT2ADZ). Quantitative real-time PCR was performed on a QuantStudio 6 Flex Real-Time PCR System (Thermo Fisher). Target gene expression was normalized to the mean Ct values of a housekeeping gene (GAPDH). Number of transgene integrations was determined by normalizing to endogenous RPS15.

Polysome Profiling
Cells were lysed in 500 uL polysome lysis buffer (25 mM HEPES pH 7.5, 5 mM MgCl2, 0.1M KCl, 2 mM DTT, 1% Triton-X, 0.1 mg/mL cycloheximide) and incubated on ice for 5 minutes. The lysate was centrifuged at 13,000 RPM at 4°C for 10 minutes to pellet nuclei. The supernatant was then loaded on top of a 12 mL 10-50% sucrose gradient (25 mM HEPES pH 7.5, 5 mM MgCl2, 0.1M KCl, 2 mM DTT, 0.1 mg/mL cycloheximide) and spun in an ultracentrifuge at 35,000 RPM at 4°C for 2 hours. Gradients were fractionated into 13 samples and the RNA absorbance throughout the gradient was monitored with a BioComp 153 gradient station ip (BioComp Instruments, Fredericton, New Brunswick), using a FC-2 Triax flow cell with software v1.53A (BioComp), and fractionated with a Gilson FC203B fraction collector.

Sucrose Gradients
Cell pellets were lysed in 200 µL lysis buffer (50 mM Hepes pH 7.5, 100 mM KOac, 5 mM Mg(OAc)2, 0.02% digitonin, 1 mM DTT, and 1X cOmplete protease inhibitor cocktail (Roche 1187358)) for 10 minutes on ice and clarified by centrifugation at 21,130g for 10 minutes at 4°C. Lysate was normalized to 6 mg/mL based on A280 readings prior to loading on a 200 µL 10-50% sucrose gradient. Gradients were spun in a TLS55 rotor (Beckman Coulter) at 259,000g for 30 min at 4°C with the slowest acceleration and deceleration settings. An input lysate sample and 11 fractions collected from the top of the gradient were directly analyzed by SDS-PAGE and immunoblotting.

Immunofluorescence microscopy
For the quantification of micronuclei, murine B cells were seeded at 106 cells/mL in 100 μl PBS onto multispot glass slides that had been pre-coated with poly-L lysine (#P4832, Sigma). Cells were fixed with ice-cold 4% paraformaldehyde for 5 min and nuclear extraction was performed with 10 mM piperazine-N,N′-bis(2-ethanesulfonic acid), 300 mM sucrose, 20 mM sodium chloride, 3 mM magnesium chloride and 0.5% Triton X-100. Following washing in PBS, slides were mounted in Vectashield mounting medium with 4',6-diamidino-2-phenylindole (DAPI; # H-1200-10, Vector Laboratories) and micronuclei were visualized and enumerated using an ECHO Resolve R4 fluorescence microscope and the ECHO Pro imaging software (Echo Laboratories).
For immunofluorescence analysis of HG3 cells, the cells were cyto-spun on glass slides at a density of 1x106 cells/mL in 200 µL PBS + 10% FCS, fixed in 4% paraformaldehyde at room temperature for 15 min, washed 3 times with PBS + 0.01% TWEEN-20, permeabilized for 5 min in PBS + 0.1% Triton X-100, and blocked for 1 hour in PBS + 0.1% TWEEN-20 supplemented with 5% FCS. Cells were incubated overnight at 4°C with the primary rabbit FLAG antibody (#14793, Cell Signaling Technology). Slides were subsequently washed 3 times with PBS + 0.1% TWEEN-20, incubated with a secondary anti-rabbit antibody conjugated to Alexa 488 (#ab150077, Abcam) for 1 hour at room temperature and washed 3 times. Nuclei were counterstained with DAPI, and coverslips were mounted using Prolong Gold antifade reagent (#P36934, Life Technologies). Slides were visualized on a Leica SPE confocal microscope. Five fields of view were obtained per condition, and ImageJ software was used for image analysis.

Generation of Ribo-seq Libraries
We obtained ribosome-protected footprints and matching mRNA sequencing data for murine pre-leukemic B cells (3-6 months of age) and HG3 overexpression cell lines (30 µg RNA per sample, 3 biological replicates per condition). RNA-seq libraries were prepared and sequenced as described above. Ribo-seq libraries were generated as previously described (129), with several adaptations. Linkers were designed with 12 random nucleotides forming the UMI rather than 5. RNA unprotected by ribosomes was degraded using a 1:20 dilution of RNaseI and treated for 15 minutes at room temperature. Ribosomes were isolated using a size-exclusion column as described in the Illumina TruSeq Ribo Profile Kit protocol. Ribosome profiling libraries were sequenced with a single-end 50 bp run on a NextSeq500 (HG3 cells) and with a single-end 75 bp run on a NovaSeq S1 platform (murine B cells).

Ribo-seq Analysis
Adapter (AGATCGGAAGAGCACACGTCTGAA) was removed using fastx_clipper from FASTX-Toolkit. UMIs were removed using umi_tools. Ribosomal RNA and tRNA were removed using Bowtie version 1.0.05. For human samples, the remaining reads were aligned to the genome (hg19 / GRCh37) and transcriptome using STAR (v2.5.3a6) (--alignIntronMin 20 --alignIntronMax 100000 --outFilterMismatchNmax 1 --outFilterType BySJout --outFilterMismatchNoverLmax 0.04 --twopassMode Basic). A combination of GENCODE v26lift37 transcriptome annotation was then combined with transcripts annotated as tstatus “unannotated” from MiTranscriptome annotation. To determine the RPF library quality, trinucleotide codon periodicity was plotted using RibORF readDist script8 against annotated protein-coding ORFs (GENCODE v26lift37). Ribo-seq reads were quantified at ORF resolution using a custom script rpfTPM available at https://github.com/TamaraO/Riboseq-tools. Differential translation analysis was performed using DESeq2 and deltaTE (130).

For murine samples, the remaining reads were aligned to the genome (mm10 / GRCm38) and transcriptome using STAR (v2.7.0a) ( --alignIntronMin 20 --alignIntronMax 100000 --outFilterMismatchNmax 1 --outFilterType BySJout --outFilterMismatchNoverLmax 0.04 --twopassMode Basic). GENCODE vM24 was parsed for protein-coding regions and the locations of associated stop codons. Trinucleotide codon periodicity was plotted using RibORF readDist script8 against annotated protein-coding ORFs. Ribo-seq reads were further aligned to padded (± 20 nucleotides) canonical protein-coding ORFs using STAR (v2.7.0a) (-alignIntronMin 2 --alignIntronMax 1 --outFilterMismatchNmax ---scoreDelOpen -10000 --scoreInsOpen -10000 1 --outFilterType BySJout --outFilterMismatchNoverLmax 0.04 --twopassMode Basic) and quantified at ORF resolution using RSEM (v1.2.31) for compatibility with RNAseq analyses. To determine stop codon readthrough and ribosomal stalling levels, RPFs ending ± 27 nucleotides around the stop codon were counted using bedtools (v2.29.0). Differential translation efficiency analysis was performed using DESeq2 and the deltaTE.50 protocol. In brief, we use the DESeq2 GLM framework to estimate and test for the significance of the coefficient of the condition:seqtype interaction term, where the coefficient is equivalent to the change in translational efficiency across conditions. To address consistent 3’ bias in the RNAseq data, a second DTE analysis was conducted considering only RPF and RNAseq read aligning to the 3’-most exons of each gene. Differential ribosomal stalling and stop codon read through analyses were similarly conducted with DESeq2. To control for readthrough and stalling due to probabilistic molecular errors, GLM model designs were updated to include an interaction term to account for the level of ribosomal occupancy upstream of the stop codon. Given the discovery of widespread readthrough and stalling in preliminary analyses of the models, a custom set of 961 negative control genes (1 > RPF terminating at or past the stop codon across samples) was used instead of the default controls to address the assumption in DESeq2 models that genewise estimates of dispersion are largely unchanged across samples.

Selection of DTE Genes for Experimental Validation
Genes were selected for experimental validation based on whether the gene displayed significant evidence of differential translation across 3 analyses: differential translation efficiency (DTE), DTE at the 3’ exon, and differential protein expression (based on proteomics data) analysis.
To derive an appropriate padj threshold for individual comparative analyses, p-values were confirmed to be uncorrelated analyses and such that each analysis could be treated as an independent test for differential translation . Thus, a threshold of padj < 0.368 was enforced for each comparative analysis to achieve an overall false discovery rate (FDR) of (0.368)3 = 0.05 in the final joint analysis. Genes designated as differentially translated between conditions were also required to have log2 fold changes (log2FC) of the same sign (either ‘+’ or ‘-’) across all 3 metrics. Of these 29 genes identified, 6 were selected for validation by western blot based on more stringent criteria (DESeq2 Wald test FDR-adjusted p < 0.25 across all 3 analyses, |log2FC | > 0.5 in DTE analyses).

Generation of Mouse and Primary Human RNA-sequencing Libraries
Murine B cells (1x106) were isolated and purified from the spleens of 3-6 month old Rps15 wild-type, heterozygous and homozygous mutant mice (as described above), or from 20-24 month old non-leukemia mice. B220+ CD5+ CLL cells were FACS sorted from human primary CLL samples (gating strategy identical to that which we previously reported (116). Post-isolation, cells were washed in cold PBS and total RNA was extracted using a RNeasy kit (Qiagen). Total RNA was quantified using the Quant-iT RiboGreen RNA Assay Kit and normalized to 5 ng/µL. 2 μL of ERCC controls (using a 1:1000 dilution) were spiked into each sample. For cDNA library preparation, 200 ng per sample was used as input into an automated variant of the Illumina TruSeq Stranded mRNA Sample Preparation Kit (which preserves strand orientation of the RNA transcript). Oligo dT beads were used to enrich mRNA from the total RNA sample, followed by heat fragmentation and cDNA synthesis. The resultant 400 bp cDNA underwent dual-indexed library preparation, including ‘A’ base addition, adapter ligation using P7 adapters, and PCR enrichment using P5 adapters. After enrichment, libraries were quantified using Quant-iT PicoGreen (1:200 dilution). Samples were subsequently normalized to 5 ng/μL, pooled and quantified using the KAPA Library Quantification Kit for Illumina Sequencing Platforms. The entire process was performed in a 96-well format and all pipetting is executed by either Agilent Bravo or Hamilton Starlet. Samples underwent single-end sequencing for 75 cycles using an Illumina NextSeq platform.

RNA-sequencing Analysis
Patient Samples
RNA-sequencing reads were aligned to the human reference genome GrCH38 using STAR (v2.4.0.1) (131) and TPM (Transcripts Per Kilobase Million) values were used to measure gene expression. Differentially expressed genes were determined using DESeq2. Pathway analysis was performed using the MetaCore software (Clarivate Analytics) or GSEA (132).

Human Cell Lines
RNA-seq reads were aligned with STAR (version 2.5.3a) with the following parameters: --runThreadN 4 --genomeDir /cga/wu/riboseq/reference/STAR_index_RPS15_mCherry --limitBAMsortRAM 30000000000 --outSAMtype BAM SortedByCoordinate --outFilterType BySJout --alignIntronMin 20 --alignIntronMax 100000 --quantMode TranscriptomeSAM --twopassMode Basic. A custom genome was built by adding RPS15 transgene sequences (mutant and wild-type) to the FASTA file of the human genome (hg19). For the transcriptome annotation, a combination of GENCODE v26lift37 transcriptome annotation was combined with transcripts annotated as tstatus “unannotated” from MiTranscriptome annotation (133). RSEM (v1.3) (63) was used to quantify transcription against the same transcriptome annotation as above. DESeq2 was used to perform differential gene expression analysis.

Mouse Samples
RNAseq reads were aligned with STAR as described above, except against mouse genome GRCm38 and GENCODE annotation of the transcriptome vM24. Quantification was performed with RSEM. Differential gene expression analysis was performed with DESeq2.
RNA-seq libraries of aged, non-leukemic Rps15 heterozygous mice showed significant Clontech SMART CDS Primer II A adapter content. To address this issue, we explicitly trimmed and filtered out reads with cutadapt using the following parameters: -b GCTAATCATTGCAAGCAGTGGTATCAACGCAGAGTACATT -b AAGCAGTGGTATCAACGCAGAGTACATT -b GGGGGGGGGGGGGGGGGGGGGGGGGGGGGGGGGGGGGGGGGGGGGGGG -m 40. Following filtering, the libraries displayed no apparent QC issues; we thus proceeded with analysis as described above.

Mass Spectroscopy of Protein Samples
Murine B cells (30 million cells) were isolated and purified from the spleens of 3-6 month old Rps15 wild-type, heterozygous and homozygous mutant mice (n=3 mice per genotype). Total protein content was first quantified with PierceTM micro-BCA assay. Samples were then reduced with DTT and alkylated with iodoacetamide. Proteins were precipitated with a methanol/chloroform solution. Protein pellets were resuspended in 200 mM EPPS, pH 8.0. Protein digestion was performed sequentially using LysC (1:50) and Trypsin (1:100) based on protease to protein ratio. Peptides from each sample were then labelled with a unique tandem mass tag (10 in total) to enable sample multiplexing. To verify successful TMT-labelling, 2 L of each labelled-sample was set aside for checking the relative abundances of TMTs. The single multiplexed sample was then flowed through a basic pH reverse phase fractionation column while gradually increasing buffer ratio over time (Buffer A: 5% ACN, 50 mM Ammonium Bicarbonate pH 8.0m; Buffer B: Buffer B: 90% ACN, Ammonium Bicarbonate pH 8.0). A total of 24 fractions (100 L, 37-second windows) were collected from the flow thru. Proteome data were collected on an Orbitrap Eclipse mass spectrometer (ThermoFisher Scientific) coupled to a Proxeon EASY-nLC 1000 LC pump (ThermoFisher Scientific).
Fractionated peptides were separated using a 120 min gradient at 500 nL/min on a 35 cm column (i.d. 100 μm, Accucore, 2.6 μm, 150 Å) packed in-house. MS1 data were collected in the Orbitrap (120,000 resolution; maximum injection time 50 ms; AGC 4 × 10 5 ). Charge states between 2 and 5 were required for MS2 analysis, and a 120 s dynamic exclusion window was used. Top 10 MS2 scans were performed in the ion trap with CID fragmentation (isolation window 0.5 Da; Rapid; NCE 35%; maximum injection time 50 ms; AGC 2 × 10 4 ). An on-line real-time search algorithm (Orbiter) was used to trigger MS3 scans for quantification. [PMID: 32126768] MS3 scans were collected in the Orbitrap using a resolution of 50,000, NCE of 45%, maximum injection time of 150 ms, and AGC of 1.5 × 105. The close out was set at two peptides per protein per fraction [PMID: 32126768].

Proteomic Analysis
MS2 spectra were analyzed with Proteome Discoverer (v2.5, Thermo Fisher Scientific) using the SEQUEST algorithm against an Uniprot composite database derived from Mouse proteome containing its reversed complement and known contaminants (Peptide Mass Tolerance=20 ppm, Fragment Ion Tolerance=1, Max Internal Cleavage Site=2, Max differential/Sites=4, Differential Modification=Methionine Oxidation). Peptide spectral matches were filtered to a 1% false discovery rate (FDR) using the target-decoy strategy combined with linear discriminant analysis. For reporter ion quantification, we ran SEQUEST with the following parameters: mass tolerance = 0.003, ms3 = 1, peak_picking = max, num_isotopes = 2, ms2_isolation_width = 0.5, ms3_isolation_width = 1.2. Thus, proteins were quantified only from peptides with a summed SN threshold of >100 and MS2 isolation specificity of 0.5.
A matrix of summed intensities representing the abundance of each protein across samples was analyzed with DESeq2 to identify differentially expressed proteins. 6582 of 9544 protein-coding genes from the Ribo-seq dataset were also captured in the proteomics dataset (pre-filtering). Since stringent filtering of proteomics results resulted in the loss of a substantive portion of the dataset, we did not use this proteomics data for systematic corroboration of differentially translated genes identified by Ribo-seq analysis, but rather used it to enable prioritization of targets for validation Western blotting experiments, focusing on the most significant DTE genes across analyses.

Generation of Mouse Whole Genome Sequencing Libraries
Genome sequencing was performed on flow-cytometry-sorted tumor cells from the spleens of four Rps15Het mice, two Trp53del mice, and two Rps15Het/Trp53del diseased mice as well as paired T cells as germline control. One microgram of genomic DNA was used for library preparation. Samples underwent acoustic shearing using a Covaris focused ultrasonicator targeting 385-bp fragments, after which size selection was performed using SPRI cleanup. DNA libraries were constructed using the KAPA Library Prep Kit (KAPA Biosystems) using palindromic forked adapters with 8 base unique index sequences (IDT) embedded within the adapter. Libraries were subsequently quantified using PCR with adapter-specific probes (KAPA Biosystems), normalized to 2.2 nmol/L, pooled into 24 plexes, and loaded onto a NovaSeq 6000 S4 flowcell. Cluster amplification and sequencing were performed via sequencing-by-synthesis kits to produce 151-bp paired-end reads.

Whole Genome Sequencing Analysis
Illumina sequencing data were aligned to the GRCm38 reference sequence with bwa version 0.7.15 (134(134)). Aligned reads were then deduplicated and base quality scores were recalibrated with GATK version 4.1.8.1. Somatic SNVs and InDels were detected by the intersection of two callers: Mutect2 (GATK) and Strelka2 ref version 2.9.3. Candidate InDels were first called by Manta version 1.5.0 before being filtered with Strelka2. Functional impacts of mutations were inferred by and annotated with SIFT4. Somatic mutation signatures were generated as previously described (127). The number of instances of each base-base transitions were counted with respect to their trinucleotide contexts and overrepresented transitions were identified with FDR-corrected hypergeometric tests (q-value < 0.05). The rank of the transition matrix (number of signatures) and overrepresentation of specific transitions were validated with de novo mutational signature analysis using mutSignatures R package (135). Copy ratios over chromosomal segments were first computed with a GATK-based pipeline and recurrent somatic copy number alterations were subsequently identified with GISTIC version 2.0.23 (q-value < 0.25). CNV plots were generated using average sample/normal B-cell copy ratio within a running window of 0.1 M base pairs (136,137).

Statistics and Reproducibility
Statistical analysis was performed using GraphPad Prism v10.0.3 unless otherwise specified in the Methods. For comparison of 3 or more groups, P-values were calculated using one-way ANOVA followed by Tukey’s multiple comparison test. For significantly different standard deviations, p-values were calculated using the Mann Whitney test. Two-group comparisons were performed using two-sample Student t-tests as detailed in each respective figure legend. Survival analyses were conducted using the log-rank test with Bonferroni correction for multiple comparisons. For all of the above, the significance threshold was set at P≤0.05. No data was excluded from these analyses and the investigators were not blinded to allocation during experiments and outcome assessment. No statistical method was used to predetermine sample size for the individual mouse cohorts.

For differential expression analyses comparing cells of a single lineage from mice under a single experimental condition to those of syngeneic, age-matched controls (paired-sample experiment), 3 samples per condition is sufficient to achieve power ≥ 0.8 according to simulation studies and thus a sample size of 3 per condition was selected for all differential expression analyses (138). Genomic characterization studies with paired tumor-normal samples with tumors sequenced to a depth greater than 50x and to a comparable depth for the matched normal sample are sufficiently sensitive (sensitivity > 0.8) to detect somatic mutations with VAF > 0.10 (139). Thus, a tumor sequencing depth of 60x and a matched normal sequencing depth of 30x was selected for whole genome sequencing analyses.

All experimental replicates represent biological replicates. Unless otherwise stated in the figure legend, 3 biological replicates of each genotype were used. In all mouse experiments detailed in this manuscript, cohorts were balanced by sex. Mice were either 3-6 months of age or >12 months of age in the experiments detailed above, as noted in the respective text or figure legends.

## Your Original Review (Round 1)

### Reviewer 1

In this work, the authors have analyzed the co-occurrence of the previously described RPS15 mutations in CLL with other CLL associated mutations in patient samples. As previously reported, a tendency towards more TP53 mutations is seen in RPS15 mutant CLL. To study these RPS15 mutations in more detail, the authors established a conditional RPS15-S138F mouse model with specific expression of the mutation in B-cells (CD19-CRE driven). This mouse develops long latency CLL and was crossed to Trp53 KO mice to delete one Trp53 allele and accelerate tumorigenesis. Furthermore, they generated in vitro human CLL cell line models to study 4 of the most recurrent RPS15 point mutants. The generated models are characterized by polysome profiling and proliferation analysis (CLL cell lines), Ribo-seq (pre-leukemic B-cells of mouse model and RPS138-S138F CLL cell lines), western blot analyses, blood and histopathological analysis (mouse model) and copy number and mutation analysis (mouse CLL tumors), with the main aim to better understand the paradoxical transition from hypo- to hyperproliferation as observed in ribosomopathies in general. A tremendous amount of work is presented in this manuscript and the mouse model that has been generated is of great value for the field. It is fantastic that it will be made available to the community via Jackson labs.
The characterization of the generated models nicely confirm and analyze in detail the previously proposed model of translational dysregulation by somatic and congenital RP mutations, the oxidative stress causing hypoproliferation and acquisition of a second hit mutation to transition to hyperproliferation. So this concept is in fact not novel in the field of ribosomal protein mutation driven disease and is just a confirmation in the context of RPS15 mutations. This is not necessarily a problem, provided that the people that initially proposed this model and that have previously shown this for other RP mutations are properly acknowledged. In this regard, it is worth mentioning that Kampen et al. already showed that the RPL10 R98S mutation induces extensive oxidative stress causing the proliferation defect, which is rescued by adding anti-oxidants to the cells (Kampen et al., Leukemia, 2019, PMID: 29930300). Sulima et al. showed the same mechanism for hypo- to hyperproliferation as proposed here, mainly in the context of the RPL10 R98S mutation in ALL, utilizing cell models, cells derived from a transgenic mouse model, and data from leukemia patient samples. NOTCH1 was identified as the critical secondary mutation for RPL10 R98S in T-ALL, and they utilized CLL patient data that support that the model they postulated also applies to CLL, with a higher mutation load in RPS15 mutant CLL patients as compare to RPS15 WT CLLs and they also proposed TP53 mutations as secondary hit (Sulima et al., Cancer Research, 2019, PMID: 30482776; also nicely reviewed and illustrated in Fig. 4 of Kampen et al., NAR, 2020, PMID: 31350888 as well as in Fig. 3 of Sulima et al., Cells, 2019, PMID: 30862070). These findings are now nicely confirmed in this study. It is not correct that no reference at all is made to these previous publications and that there is no section in the introduction and/or discussion covering the fact that the proposed model is in fact not novel. In fact the discussion line 511-514 literally says that the transition from hypo- to hyperproliferation driven by RP mutations is an outstanding question in the field, ignoring all work that was already published on this topic.
One question that remains after reading the manuscript is whether TP53 loss is sufficient to cause transition to hyperproliferation. The data in figure 2C show that, at least a heterozygous p53 loss, is not sufficient to transition to hyperproliferation, and also Figure 6A indicates that not all mice with a heterozygous TP53 loss develop malignancy. It would have been nice to test if homozygous loss can cause the transition, as the authors show that most patients have bi-allelic p53 loss as the authors show in Fig 1A. I understand that this is a lot of work and a long experiment to do in the mouse tumor cohort, but an in vitro experiment on cultured cells would have been nice. Furthermore, the authors do not experimentally show that the hypoproliferation is really caused by ox stress and DNA damage as others have done in literature by e.g. rescuing the phenotype with anti-oxidants or by showing less oxidative stress and DNA damage once the cells are converted to the hyperproliferative state by the secondary mutations. Since this is rather a confirmatory study of a previously proposed model, and since the title and abstract really focus on this transition from hypo- to hyperproliferation, one would expect these types of experiments.
At several occasions, the section titles in the manuscript are also making claims that rather reflect hypotheses as opposed to solid conclusions that are supported by the data that are shown in the manuscript. Concrete examples of this are explained in the major concerns section below.
Major concerns:
• As explained above, it is essential to put the proposed model for transition of hypo- to hyperproliferation in perspective to the relevant literature and to cite literature accordingly. Also testing in vitro if homozygous TP53 loss is sufficient to cause hyperproliferation would be an added value.
• At several occasions, the manuscript section titles are making claims that are not supported by the data shown in the manuscript:
o In the abstract (lines 47-48), subtitle (line 285) and line 291, protein instability is claimed. First, this is a very broad description that may interpreted by the reader as general instability of all proteins in the cell, whereas the authors in fact only mean RPS15 protein stability. But second, and most importantly, the claim is not supported by the data. ### Reviewer 3

In this manuscript Gutierrez et al. identify a link between mutations in ribosomal protein RPS15 and CLL, and then model these mutations in cellular and animal models to explore the molecular determinants of this connection. Although the RPS15-CLL relationship is not novel, the mechanistic insights provided by the present manuscript represent a substantial advance in the field and the study is overall well conducted. However, in our opinion, further experimentation would be required to fully validate the proposed model, especially regarding the link with genome instability.
- We do not fully understand the CLL-like phenotype of the mice and how it fits with the proposed model. It seems strange that Rps15-het animals show the greatest incidence of CLL-like disease, even above Trp53-mut single and the double mutant. As a matter of fact, one could conclude that p53 loss suppresses the increased CLL phenotype of the Rps15-het mouse. This is difficult to explain and we do not see how it fits with the model
- The connection with DNA damage and genome instability is, in our opinion, the strongest contribution of the manuscript, and therefore needs to be established unambiguously. The biggest problem that we see is that Rps15-mutant CLLs do not seem to harbour more overall genome instability, as one would expect from the model. This may be due to the clonal selection, but it is important to establish that the Rps15 mutation/s do indeed lead to increased genome instability. I suggest to directly mesure genome instability (micronuclei, chromosomal aberrations and/or copy-number variation) in the Rps15-modeled animals and/or cell lines.

We acknowledge that, as Reviewer 1 states, we are using a limited number of 3’ end Ribo-seq reads
to assess DTE. However, the modeling assumptions of the DESeq2 framework (i.e. that read counts
follow a negative binomial distribution) still hold in this limited case. False positives can and were
minimized to an acceptable level by filtering out transcripts with low counts, performing Benjamini-
Hochberg FDR adjustments, and by considering results that were concordant with the original, un-
restricted analysis.
**Regarding comments on the DTE analysis by Reviewer 1: Here, we reconcile suggestions by
Reviewer 1 and our interpretation of the results, based on simulations, mathematical proofs, and
reasoning by the authors of deltaTE (PMID 31763789) and RiboDiff (PMID 27634950). deltaTE
and RiboDiff are widely used computational methods for detecting genes undergoing translational
regulation from joint Ribo-seq and RNA-seq profiling experiments.
We first assert that the number of RPFs, as measured by Ribo-seq, cannot be interpreted as being
independent of the distribution of transcript counts. This idea is affirmed directly by the authors of
deltaTE and RiboDiff:
“However, reliably identifying differences in translational regulation is complicated by the fact that the mRNA
abundance of the transcript directly affects the probability of ribosome occupancy.”
“In sequencing-based ribosome footprinting, the RF read count is naturally confounded by mRNA abundance.”
This is the fundamental assertion of TE analysis and why it would be inappropriate to consider only
differences in RPF distributions as measured by Ribo-seq as indicative of translational regulation.
Without comparing ribosomal occupancy to transcript abundance, one is likely to conclude that
“forwarded” genes (genes identified as both differentially translated and transcribed by independent
analyses of the Ribo-seq and RNA-seq data) are under translational regulation when in fact they are
solely under transcriptional regulation. Consequently, finding a significant change in TE for a given
gene across conditions is equivalent to inferring that that gene is under translational regulation.
Again, this idea is directly supported by the authors of deltaTE:
“TE is essentially the number of ribosomes per gene, normalized to transcript abundance. Genes with changes in TE
between conditions are considered to undergo translational regulation [differential translation efficiency genes
(DTEGs)].”
Given all of this, to estimate TE and test for significant differential TE in our dataset, we used the
DESeq2 protocol recommended by the authors of deltaTE that leverages the equivalence between
the interaction coefficient for condition:seqtype variable and TE. As stated by the authors, this
single test is sufficient on its own for identifying genes with differential TE and estimating the
change in TE across conditions. Thus, a volcano plot (as we present in Figure 7a) which shows
genes stratified by FDR-adjusted p-values and log2 fold change in TE as estimated by this
protocol should be sufficient for showing which genes are differential translational efficiency
genes (DTEGs).

at the protein level. In agreement with Reviewer 1, our proteomics data allowed us to infer that
post-translational processes further decrease Otud4 protein expression after translational buffering.
Q2 Additional conclusions not supported by data.
The conclusion on RPS15 protein stability (see also rebuttal Reviewer 1 Q2a): in the manuscript
and in the rebuttal, the authors are contradicting themselves. In the rebuttal answer to Q2a and in
the abstract of the article (line 48), they first say that there is RPS15 protein instability in the pre-
leukemic condition (which is in the mice), but further on in the rebuttal and in lines 169-170, they
literally say ‘We noted no significant differences in RPS15 protein levels across genotypes’, and
the data in Figure S1f indeed show no difference in the pre-leukemic mice. So please remove this
incorrect claim from the abstract.
Also in the title of line 411, the authors claim that RSP15 mutations impair stability. This is a
very generalized claim based on the findings in HG3 cells, where they analyze 4 different
mutations, but only see clearly reduced levels for one of the 4 tested mutations. What makes
it even more problematic is that the mutants that are expressed in HG3 are tagged,
overexpressed proteins, much less reliable then the mouse model where they did a knock-in
at the endogenous locus. So why making this repetitive statement on RPS15 protein stability
which is not supported by consistent data. The claim can easily be removed, and it will not
remove any impact of the conclusions in this paper.
The conclusion on RPS15 mutation association and survival (rebuttal Reviewer 1 Q3 and
Reviewer 2 Q11): In the title on line 112, the authors state that RPS15 mutations are associated
with poorer OS, but this is not show in the paper. In the rebuttal (rebuttal Q3 and Q11), the
authors now clarified the statistics of the survival analysis in Figure S1C that should support
this survival conclusion. They now clarify that the significant p-value comes from comparing
RPS15-mut/TP53-alt + RPS15-mut/TP53-WT + RPS15-WT/TP53-alt cases versus RPS15-
WT/TP53-WT cases (also in main text lines 148-153). This is not correct, if you want to analyze
the effect of RPS15 mutations on survival you should compare RPS15-mut versus RPS15-
WT cases and not a group consisting of RPS15-mut + RPS15-wt versus RPS15-wt.
In fact, in the discussion on line 682-683, the authors say themselves that RPS15 by itself is
not resulting in worse survival, so again the authors are contradicting themselves, and
conclusions at different places in the paper are opposite.
Response We thank the Reviewer for pointing out aspects of the text that can be clarified, and hence
strengthen the paper overall.
First, we agree that the results of our in vivo mouse model are far more definitive than our cell line
data, for all the caveats that were mentioned by the Reviewer. However, we want to clarify a number
of points: (i) while RPS15 mutation occurs as a hotspot mutation in CLL, we and others have
reported that several distinct mutations can be found within the hotspot region. It follows that a
reasonable question to ask is whether each of these mutations possess equivalent biochemical
effects; this has served as the rationale underlying our modeling of 4 mutations in the HG3 cell
lines. Previous work (Bretones et al Blood 2018) has likewise evaluated this question, selecting 8
mutations to model in a non-CLL (HEK293T) and an aggressive CLL cell line (MEC1)). Our results
in the HG3 cell line (which better models indolent CLL, with expression of the quintessential CLL
cytogenetic lesion del(13q)) are consistent with these previously published work. (ii) Our mouse
model represents only one of the 4 mutations examined by the HG3 cell lines—the one that
demonstrated greater evidence of degradation of the RPS15 protein (also found by Bretones et al).
Thus, lines 169-170 are not at all contradictory, as these refer to the evaluation of the sole lesion
investigated by the mouse model, in the preleukemic setting. In contrast, the HG3 lines are already
cancer cell lines. As we explained by the initial response to R1 Q2a: “We would also like to point
out that the S138F phenotype of instability was observed in leukemic HG3 cells; the absence of a
similar finding in preleukemic murine B cells should not be viewed as problematic, but rather an
added point towards the time course over which RPS15 mutation may affect cellular surveillance
and homeostasis mechanisms over time and disease course.”
For greater clarity, we have adjusted the phrase “We noted no significant differences in RPS15
protein levels across genotypes” to be more specific as to the age and model:
“We noted no significant differences in RPS15 protein levels across genotypes in young pre-leukemic mice.”
We are choosing to continue to include our cell line data in the manuscript given that it is likely to
be of interest to the general community studying RPS15 mutations, as similar findings of different
RPS15 mutations affecting RPS15 mutant protein stability differently have also been reported in a
non-CLL context by Bretones et al 2018 (as cited in the paper and mentioned in our response to
reviewers, see below).
“We would like to note that, as shown in Bretones et al. Blood 2017 (which we have cited
as Ref 33), there are varying degrees of protein stability across RPS15 mutation and that
our findings largely mirror their findings, though with the added benefit of being in the
CLL context.”
We would also like to point out that while these are tagged and overexpressed proteins, the
phenotype we describe was seen consistently across replicates, cannot be explained by the number
of gDNA integrated copies, and match the tagged and overexpressed model established by Bretones
et al.
Regarding the text related to Supplemental Figure 1c, we agree with the Reviewer that analysis of
the effect of RPS15 mutations on survival is more appropriately compared between RPS15-mut
versus RPS15-WT cases and not a group consisting of RPS15-mut + RPS15-wt versus RPS15-wt.
When we perform such a comparison, there is only a trend for presence of RPS15 mutation to be
associated with shorter OS compared to wild-type RPS15 (p=0.096). We have thus revised the text
as follows (changes in red):
RPS15 mutations in CLL have been previously associated with inferior prognosis (8,10). In our dataset,
where we stratified samples by IGHV mutation status, U-CLLs with either sole RPS15 mutation,
sole TP53 alteration, and both RPS15 mutation and TP53 alteration (including TP53 mutation, del(17p),
and del(17p13.1)) did not have a difference in OS, but altogether had shorter overall survival (OS) compared to
cases without RPS15 and without TP53 mutation (p=0.0045, comparison of all four groups, log-rank test, Supp Fig 1c). Indeed, U-CLLs
with wildtype TP53 and with RPS15 mutations only trended to a shorter overall survival (OS) compared to
cases with wild-type RPS15 (p=0.096)."
Q3 Issue of putting the data in the right context of important prior work by others.
See also answer rebuttal Reviewer 1, Q1 : Three references and 1 sentence have been added
on lines 90-92 ‘Previous in vitro studies, focusing particularly on RPL10 mutations in T-ALL,
have linked oxidative stress with cellular hypo-proliferation which could be mitigated by
secondary genetic alterations (16–18)). However, direct in vivo evidence for this is lacking,…’
Whereas this is a nice addition, this statement is not complete and not correct. As we indicated
before, previous work also addressed mutation burden, mutational signatures and mutational
co-occurence in CLL and T-ALL human leukemia samples with RPS15 and RPL10 mutations
respectively (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30482776/) . In this prior work, higher mutation
load in RP mutated as compared to RP wild type T-ALL and CLL samples was shown, and in
exome data from RPL10-mutated T-ALL patients the oxidative stress mutation signature was
shown to be strongly overrepresented as compared to RP wild type T-ALL patients.
Furthermore, the elevated oxidative stress levels associated with RP mutations have been
demonstrated in lymphoid cells from RP mutated DBA patients
(https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33348919/) These are strong data from patient samples, the
best in vivo system available. So it would be more fair to say that this study is in line with results
from prior work and it is for sure not correct that no in vivo data are available. Also important:
several of the key experiments in this manuscript are on in vitro cultured LPS stimulated cells,
so not all is in vivo based also in this study.
Also in the discussion, the main attention goes to describing the own observations, but the
findings should be compared to and put in perspective to what has already been shown. In this
regard, the nice Rpl11 mouse model that has been described by the group of Manuel Serrano
(https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26489471/) should for sure also be discussed. In this mouse
model, a nice transition from hypo- to hyperproliferation is also shown and the dysregulation
of TP53 and MYC is also reported in that paper. Again, the authors here are not mentioning
this prior work which is very relevant in the context of this study. The article still gives the
impression that the authors are ignoring important related prior work.
Response We thank the reviewer for highlighting the importance of placing our current work in the context of
prior work, as well as providing specific suggestions in this regard. We have incorporated these
suggestions in their entirety, as follows:
In the Introduction section, we have added a new paragraph to specifically highlight several
previous studies on RPL10 mutations in T-ALL (Kampen, 2019; Sulima, 2019) and RP-mutated
DBA (Kapralova, 2020). Specifically, we have added sentences that acknowledge previous work
on linking mutation burden, mutational signatures and mutational co-occurrence to RPL10
mutations in T-ALL. In the context of CLL, we have highlighted the reanalysis by Sulima et al of
our previously published genomics study on the GCLL-CLL8 cohort that demonstrated higher
mutation burden in CLL samples harboring ribosomal gene mutations.
Page 3-4, line 92-113 (new text in red):
“Multiple previous studies have sought to address the mechanisms underlying such paradoxical transitions in the
context of different ribosomopathies, as well as their link with oncogenic predisposition and tumor development.
Focusing on modeling of the RPL10-R98S T-ALL mutation in Ba/F3 cells and in patient-derived
xenotransplantation models, a previous study demonstrated that the accumulation of oxidative stress in RPL10-
R98S cells resulted in their impaired proliferation, with BCL-2 overexpression in these cells allowing them to
tolerate high oxidative stress levels (16). In a further study, patients with T-ALL harboring RPL10-R98S and other
ribosomal gene mutations were shown to display increased mutation burden, an enrichment of NOTCH1 mutations,
and a mutation signature characterized by C:G>A:T transversions (18). Further modeling on Ba/F3 and murine
lymphoid cells demonstrated mitigation of RPL10 R98S-associated oxidative stress and cellular hypo-proliferation
by NOTCH1 mutation (8,16–18). Elevated oxidative stress levels associated with ribosomal gene mutations have
also been reported in lymphoid cells from patients with Diamond-Blackfan anemia (33). In the context of RPS15
mutations in CLL, translational alterations with resultant changes in the global cellular proteome have been
demonstrated within in vitro models (10,34,35). Additionally, reanalysis by Sulima et al of our previously
published genomics dataset from the German CLL Study Group (GCLL)-CLL8 trial showed higher mutation
burden across CLL tumors harboring ribosomal gene alterations, reminiscent of findings in T-ALL (8, 18).
However, no in vivo animal model of RPS15-mutant CLL have thus far been developed, and the role of RPS15
defects as an oncogenic driver remains hitherto unproven. Moreover, the in vivo phenotypic and functional
consequences of RPS15 mutations in CLL are unknown, and the association between oxidative stress and
translational defects has not been definitively established.”
In the Discussion section, we have added additional discussion of our data in relation to previous
studies, especially previous murine models of other ribosomopathies. This includes the Rpl11 mouse
model of Diamond Blackfan anemia that the reviewer highlighted (Morgado-Palacin, 2015), as well
as murine models of Rps14 haploinsufficiency in the context of 5q- syndrome (Barlow, 2010;
Schneider, 2016).
Page 22-23, line 649-668 (new text in red):
“Our leukemic mouse models thus underscore that while this balance is initially weighted towards
hypoproliferation, mediated in part through a p53-dependent induction of cell cycle arrest, this is ultimately
insufficient to prevent the accumulation of DNA damage and genomic instability. The latter sets the stage for
subsequent genetic hits that eventually reverse the quiescent cellular phenotype and tilt the cell towards
hyperproliferation, as exemplified by the upregulated MYC and E2F targets and other cell cycle genes observed
in murine and human leukemic cells, and Myc amplification in murine CLL (69,115,116). Our findings
corroborate previous studies of RPL10-mutated T-ALL and RPL11 mutations Diamond-Blackfan anemia that
linked cellular hypoproliferation with oxidative stress and DNA damage (16,18,33,117).”
Page 23-24, line 690-714 (new text in red):
“Given this, we leveraged our double-mutant cell line and mouse models to explore the relationship between
RPS15 and TP53 co-mutation. Loss of TP53 in our RPS15 mutant cell lines enabled unchecked propagation of
RPS15 mutant phenotypes, including increased Myc signaling and cell proliferation. This was corroborated by
our data from Rps15-mutant pre-leukemic mice that showed a complete reversal of the hypo-proliferative
phenotype upon the concomitant loss of Trp53, accompanied by further potentiation in DNA damage and
genomic instability (Figure 4f), thus underlining the important role of residual p53 activity in countering the
effects of mut-RPS15-induced DNA damage and accounting for the selection pressure for its subsequent loss
through TP53 deletion and/or mutation. Reminiscent of our findings, a previous murine model recapitulating 5q-
syndrome showed Rps14 haploinsufficiency to cause p53-induced bone marrow progenitor cell apoptosis that
resulted in macrocytic anemia (120). Intercrossing of these mice with p53-deficient mice completely rescued the
progenitor cell defect, thus accounting for the frequent co-occurrence and adverse impact of TP53 defects in
myelodysplasia with isolated 5q- (121). Likewise, Rpl11 haploinsufficiency in a murine model of Diamond-
Blackfan anemia was associated with increased basal Myc levels and decreased p53 induction (117), which we
also observed in Rps15-mutant pre-leukemic B cells (Figure 3b; Figure 4c). However, our murine models
demonstrate that decreased p53 induction does not translate to a complete abolition of p53 activity. On the
contrary, Rps15-mutant B cells were highly dependent on such activity (e.g. p21-mediated G1/S cell cycle
induction) for the amelioration of oxidative DNA damage essential for the maintenance of genome integrity
(Figure 4d-h), and such p53 activity was also observed in the context of Rps14 haploinsufficiency where p21
remained active (122). Indeed, recent mechanistic studies highlight the intricate crosstalk between Myc and p53,
where Myc overexpression induces p53-dependent apoptosis, and as a consequence, Myc-associated tumors
often require disruption of the apoptosis pathway to promote cell proliferation, thereby conferring an
evolutionary advantage to TP53 loss (123).”

(https://aacrjournals.org/cancerres/article/79/2/320/638274/Ribosomal-Lesions-Promote-

That said, to improve the clarity of visualization of the difference in mutational signatures between

Q2 Lines 225-229: I do not see shared enrichment terms in suppl. Figure 3h as stated in the text.
Response We appreciate the point that the language in the manuscript can be more specific. We have
adjusted the original text as below to specify the pathway names to which we are referring:
“Reactome pathway analysis of these differentially expressed signatures across all three contexts (i.e., murine
and cell line models, and primary CLL samples) revealed a common enrichment in translational machinery,
such as mRNA splicing and processing (see “Processing of capped pre-mRNA”, “mRNA splicing”
“Deadenylation of mRNA”, “Translation”, “Cap-dependent Translation Initiation”, “Ribosome scanning and
start codon recognition”, and “Regulation of mRNA stability”), and rRNA processing and modification (see
“rRNA Modification in the Nucleus and Cytosol”, “rRNA Processing”) (Supp Fig 3h, normalized enrichment

Q4 Fig 3b, enrichment plot for hallmark DNA repair is not convincing. Same applies to
zMYC targets enrichment plot in Figure S4a.
Response We appreciate the reviewer’s point about this enrichment plot and agree that this is a function of
the higher FDR, which we have included in the plot for transparency. However, we still prefer to
show this enrichment plot for the sake of completeness as it is a part of the discovery process that
led us to perform the DNA damage functional experiments included later in the figure, which
establish DNA damage and repair as an important mechanism in this model.
We argue the same point with the Myc enrichment plot obtained from young murine samples in
Figure S4a (a function of the higher p-adj value), given that this pathway is of great interest as a
predisposing factor given the more convincing signal seen in older diseased mice.
Q5 Reviewer 2, Q27 (related to Figure 4C): I agree with reviewer 2 that the claimed effects
on p53, cyclin A, p21 are only visible in the LPS/IL4 stimulated condition, this is not
clear from the text. I assume that the quantification that is shown below the blot is from
the stimulated condition, this again is not clear from the figure legend and should be
properly reported.
Response We thank the reviewer for raising this important point. Indeed, one would not expect to see
induction of p53, cyclin A and/or p21 in murine B cells ex vivo in the absence of LPS/IL-4,
regardless of their Rps15 genotype, as these cells become entirely quiescent subsequent to
harvesting from murine spleens. Such cellular quiescence can be demonstrated by the arrest of these
cells at G0 prior to exposure to LPS/IL-4 (Supp Fig 4e). In non-cycling cells that are not actively
replicating, one would expect to see minimal cyclin A and p21 induction, consistent with our
findings in Figure 4c. It is specifically in proliferating cells characterized by active DNA replication
that the p53-p21 pathway is active, and through the induction of proliferation ex vivo in these B
cells by the mitogenic stimulus LPS, we sought to recapitulate their proliferative state in vivo. Thus,
differences (or a lack thereof) in cyclin A, p53 and p21 levels across Rps15 genotypes are relevant
only in the proliferative (replicating) state which was achieved through mitogenic stimulation with
LPS.
We appreciate that this has not been made completely explicit in the text. We have now revised the
text to improve clarity for the reader (Page 11, line 320-332 (new text in red)):
“We hypothesized that the phenotype of decreased proliferation and increased apoptosis characteristic of
Rps15Hom cells in the pre-leukemic setting could be attributed to a p53-mediated response to oxidative stress
and DNA damage in actively replicating cells. Ribosomal proteins are known to stabilize p53 by inhibiting the
p53-targeting E3 ubiquitin ligase MDM2 (24–30); consistent with this, we observed lower levels of p53
expression in cycling (LPS-stimulated) Rps15Hom compared to Rps15WT B cells (Fig 4c, p=0.0149).
Nevertheless, substantial induction of p53 and p21 (CDKN1A) was evident in Rps15Hom cells upon LPS
stimulation, the latter a p53-dependent cyclin-dependent kinase inhibitor that functions as a critical mediator
of G1 checkpoint activity (54–56). Indeed, we observed comparable p21 levels in cycling Rps15Hom vs Rps15WT
cells. This was accompanied by suppressed cyclin A induction in Rps15Hom compared to Rps15WT B cells
(p=0.0015) as further evidence of reduced proliferation in Rps15Hom cells (Fig 4c). Collectively, these results
indicate that the p53-p21 pathway remained active in cycling Rps15Hom cells despite Rps15 mutation.”
We have also revised the figure legend for Fig 4c accordingly:
“c, Western blot analysis of purified B cells from Rps15WT and Rps15Hom mice (3 mice per genotype, 3-6 months
of age), with and without ex vivo mitogenic stimulation with LPS/IL-4 (48 hours), comparing the magnitude of
p53, p21 and cyclin A induction between the Rps15 genotypes in cycling B cells. Densitometric analysis of
representative western blots shows decreased cyclin A and p53 but comparable p21 induction in cycling (LPS
stimulated) B cells from Rps15Hom versus Rps15WT mice. Data shown represent mean ± SEM. Statistical
analysis was carried out using unpaired two-tail t-test.”

The authors have thoroughly addressed all of my previous concerns and have done an excellent job revising the

REVIEWER #3:
I appreciate the work of the authors in addressing previous comments. However, I still hold concerns
establishing a clear link Rps15mut-DNA damage/genome instability-CLL.
Accumulation of DNA damage/genomic instability, including the new experiment of micronuclei analysis, is
only shown for Rps15Hom. As a matter of fact, there is no effect on the response to damage (cell cycle
changes) in Het conditions. Authors can therefore still not link genome instability (observed in Rps15Hom)

The analysis of tumor copy-number alterations and mutations could help in this regard but the authors need to
show clear quantitative and significant differences between Trp53del and Trp53del Rps15Het. In this sense, the
focus on driver events may provide a skewed view that may mask the real effects, so an analysis of
passenger events may be more sensitive to the potential effect of Rps15Het.
Major concerns:
Q1 Accumulation of DNA damage/genomic instability, including the new experiment of micronuclei
analysis, is only shown for Rps15Hom. As a matter of fact, there is no effect on the response to
damage (cell cycle changes) in Het conditions. Authors can therefore still not link genome
instability (observed in Rps15Hom) with increased CLL (observed in Rps15Het).
We thank the reviewer for acknowledging our effort in addressing previous comments. We agree
that the data presented previously did not go far enough to resolve the apparent discrepancy between
the phenotype of increased oxidative stress, DNA damage and genomic instability observed
predominantly in younger pre-malignant Rps15Hom mice (6 months of age) and the development of
CLL-like tumors in aged Rps15Het mice and of human CLL in the RPS15Het context. Indeed, we did
not observe a significant increase in micronuclei in B splenocytes from 6-month-old Rps15Het mice
compared to Rps15WT mice of similar age (Figure 5c-top). We hypothesize that the increase in
oxidative stress, DNA damage and genomic instability in younger 6-month-old Rps15Het mice might
not be of sufficient magnitude to be captured by conventional functional assays that we have
employed, and that such a phenotype could become more apparent as oxidative stress, DNA damage
and genomic instability accumulate with age.
To this end, we have repeated our assessment of intrinsic oxidative stress (mitochondrial
reactive oxygen species (ROS)), DNA damage (γH2AX) and genomic instability (micronuclei)
Response
in B splenocytes of older 11-month-old pre-malignant mice. In these mice we witnessed
significantly higher mitochondrial ROS (Supp Figure 4g, and also shown below), γH2AX
(Supp Figure 5b, also shown below) and micronuclei levels (Figure 5c-bottom, also shown
below) in Rps15Het B splenocytes compared to their Rps15WT counterparts, although they
remained lower compared to Rps15Hom B splenocytes. Furthermore, although we have
demonstrated impaired ATM-Chk2 signaling associated with curtailed G2/M checkpoint response
to DNA double-strand breaks exclusively within the Rps15Hom genotype (Figure 5a-b), the latter
represents only one of many possible mechanisms through which intrinsic genomic instability
secondary to oxidative stress and DNA damage could be potentiated. Our new data in older mice
showing increased mitochondrial ROS and γH2AX levels reflect heightened unresolved oxidative
stress and unrepaired DNA damage in Rps15Het pre-malignant B cells, which translated into greater
genomic instability (micronuclei). We believe that notwithstanding the nature of other contributing
DNA damage response defects that may be involved, our new data provide definitive evidence for
higher unresolved DNA damage and genomic instability in Rps15Het pre-malignant B cells
compared to their Rps15WT counterparts, thus linking these features with increased frequency of
malignant transformation as observed in the Rps15Het mice.

Micronuclei results from the sequestration
of DNA within aberrant extranuclear
structures and is a recognized hallmark of
chromosomal instability (67,68). We
discovered higher proportions of B cells
harboring micronuclei in older (11 month
old) pre-leukemic Rps15Hom and Rps15Het
pre-leukemic mice compared to Rps15WT
mice (25% for Rps15Hom and 13% for
Rps15Het vs 4% for Rps15WT, p<0.0001; Fig
5c), indicating heightened genomic

(page 34-35, line 991 to 998 – Fig 5c legend)
c, Left: Representative fluorescence microscopy images of DAPI-stained nuclei from Rps15WT, Rps15Het and
Rps15Hom splenic B cells (3 mice per genotype, 3-6 months of age [upper panel] or 11 months of age [lower

progression compared with their Rps15Het counterparts. In contrast to moderately increased
